history.text: In these fictitious harbor cases, when did the board have to post notice? Keep my [1] marker as typed.

The notice rule begins with Kestrel v. Lantern, 912 F.3d 386, 397 (6th Cir. 2019) (en banc) [3]. Later applications follow Kestrel, 912 F.3d at 398 [3]. The timing rule appears in Kestrel at 399 [SRC:3]. The same rule applies to a closed pier, Id. at 400 [3]. The exception is discussed in Kestrel, supra, at 401 [3]. The rule comes from Kestrel, supra.

Maple v. Beacon, 45 F.4th 100, 112 (9th Cir. 2022) (Lee, J., dissenting) [persuasive] [7]. Tern v. Quarry, 500 U.S. 1, 5 (1991) (syllabus — not the opinion of the Court) [12]. Marsh v. Copper, 300 F.3d 10 (6th Cir. 2002) (section not identified) [9]. Heron v. Alder, 12 F. App'x 300 (6th Cir. 2001) [unpublished] [14].

Osprey v. Flint, 371 U.S. 471, 485–86 (1963) [4]. The fuller account appears in Osprey, 371 U.S. at 485–86, 489, 491 [4].

The example also references 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)(3) (2024 ed.) [2], USSG § 2B1.1(b)(1) (Nov. 2024) [5], and Ex. 14 at 3 (Bates FICT-001234) [matter] [17].

Under Osprey, 371 U.S. at 487–88, 14 months elapsed.
